title: Articles, Determiners and Quantification
orientation: Articles and quantity words help readers identify what you mean and how much of it you are discussing. A small change from a to the, or from few to a few, can alter the message even when the main vocabulary stays the same. This lesson develops those choices through reference, countability and context rather than a list of isolated substitutions. Start by asking whether a noun is being used countably and whether the intended referent is identifiable. Then compare general statements, institutional expressions and quantities. Offers, measurements and regional conventions are particularly useful checks against oversimplified rules. The advanced layers distinguish definiteness from specificity and explore the scope of negation. After the guided examples, write your own arrangements and descriptions, explaining why each determiner fits its context. The aim is a reasoned choice, not guessing which small word sounds most formal.
outcomes: Choose a/an by sound and distinguish indefinite form from specificity.
Explain identifiable and generic references using articles or zero article.
Apply conventional institutional and geographical article patterns with regional qualification.
Use distributive determiners and quantifiers with compatible noun senses.
Explain the meaning differences in some/any, few/a few and little/a little.

modules.title: Articles, identification and general reference
modules.definition: Articles are a, an and the. A/an introduces one member of a countable class; the normally signals that the intended referent is identifiable in the situation or discourse. Zero article means that no article occurs, not that the noun phrase has no grammatical structure.
foundation: Start with a singular count use: a report, an interview. A/an depends on the next sound rather than the next letter: a university, an hour, an unusual report and a useful report. The next sound may belong to an adjective, not to the noun. An introduces one unspecified member for the listener, but the speaker may already know which one: I spoke to a specialist yesterday can describe a specific person. Do not confuse indefinite form with a speaker having no particular individual in mind.
intermediate: Use the when the intended referent is identifiable. A visitor rang the bell. The visitor asked for directions introduces the person and then refers back. First mention is not the only source of identification: Please close the door can work when the relevant door is obvious. A bridging link also helps: We entered a house. The kitchen was bright. The kitchen is identifiable through its relationship to the house even though kitchen has not appeared before. If several doors or kitchens are equally relevant, add enough description to establish which is meant.
advanced: General reference has several structures. Tigers are mammals uses a bare plural for the class generally. A tiger is a mammal describes a representative member. The tiger is endangered presents the species as a category; this singular generic pattern is conventional but cannot replace every bare-plural generalisation mechanically. Noncount nouns often have zero article for general reference: Water is essential. The water in this bottle is warm identifies a particular quantity. A noun being abstract does not itself forbid the: Justice matters, but the justice of the decision was disputed.
expert: Definiteness, specificity and uniqueness are related ideas, not synonyms. The author of this report can identify a unique role even if the reader does not know the author’s name. I need a book about wetlands can be nonspecific, whereas I bought a book about wetlands may refer to a particular purchased book. Context decides whether a description sufficiently identifies its referent; grammar does not supply a universal first-mention checklist. A/an normally accompanies a singular count use, but determiners and constructions permit other patterns, developed below. The article belongs to the noun phrase and does not tell you the noun’s function by itself.

patterns.meaning: One member of a class, with the article chosen by the following sound.
The writer presents the referent as recoverable from context, discourse or descriptive information.

examples.sentence: A pilot phoned. The pilot left a message.
examples.analysis: First indefinite mention is followed by an identifiable reference to the same person.

examples.sentence: The roof of the library needs repairs.
examples.analysis: The of-phrase helps identify the intended roof without an earlier mention of roof.

examples.sentence: Copper conducts electricity; the copper in this cable is damaged.
examples.analysis: The first clause is generic; the second identifies a particular material quantity.

contrasts.a: I am looking for a particular engineer whom I met yesterday.
contrasts.b: I am looking for an engineer who can repair this device.
contrasts.note: Both are grammatical. The first describes a specific person; the second can mean any suitable engineer.

exceptions: Letters alone do not decide a/an: an MP uses the initial sound /em/, while a USB cable begins with /juː/. Accent and how an abbreviation is spoken can change the appropriate choice.

mistakes.reason: University begins with a consonant sound despite its initial vowel letter.

mistakes.problem: The oxygen is necessary for human life. Intended: oxygen generally.
mistakes.repair: Oxygen is necessary for human life.
mistakes.reason: A general noncount reference normally uses zero article; the would need an identifying context.

glossary.definition: Presentation of a referent as identifiable in context.
glossary.example: The report on your desk identifies a particular report.

glossary.definition: Reference to a particular entity rather than any suitable member of a class.
glossary.example: A certain visitor called refers to a particular visitor.

modules.title: Articles with institutions, names and abstract nouns
modules.definition: Article patterns depend on noun meaning, conventional names and the activity being described. A geographical or institutional expression must be learned as a whole pattern, with regional alternatives identified where they affect interpretation.
foundation: Compare school as an institution and a school as a building or organisation. The children are at school normally describes participation as pupils. I waited outside the school identifies a particular location. British English commonly uses in hospital for a patient, while in the hospital can identify a building; American English commonly uses in the hospital for the patient meaning too. Bed has a conventional zero-article sleep use: go to bed. These are established constructions, not evidence that every building used for its purpose loses its article. A person may go to the bank for ordinary banking.
intermediate: Names have conventional article patterns. Many personal names, cities, countries and individual mountains have zero article: Sana, Karachi, Pakistan and Mount Kenya. Some country names conventionally include the, including the United Kingdom and the United States. Rivers, seas, oceans and mountain ranges commonly take the: the Indus, the Arabian Sea and the Himalayas. A plural name or a descriptive political name can therefore differ from a simple country name. Learn the complete name, rather than infer the article from national importance or size. Local institutional names also have their own conventions.
advanced: Abstract and material nouns can be general, specific or conventionally countable in different senses. Education is important is general; the education she received was expensive identifies particular education. She had an excellent education uses a recognised count interpretation of an educational experience. The same contrast explains life and a life, knowledge and a detailed knowledge of the region. Do not add a/an to ordinary information or advice merely because an adjective intervenes. Useful advice remains noncount. Meals, languages, sports and subjects often have zero article in general activity uses, but a restrictive description can identify an instance: the lunch we ordered arrived late.
expert: Article omission also occurs in names, headlines, notices, coordinated expressions and role descriptions. They elected her chair is a recognised complement construction; it does not license They bought chair for an ordinary object. Proper names may acquire modified or count uses, as a young Mozart or the London of her childhood, and such expressions need contextual interpretation. British and American conventions should be described at the construction level. At university is a useful British educational pattern; at college is common in American contexts. A writer choosing a particular national convention should preserve it while recognising legitimate standard alternatives.

patterns.form: at school / in hospital in relevant British institutional uses
patterns.meaning: The noun evokes the institutional activity or participant status.
The phrase identifies a particular instance, kind or quantity.

examples.sentence: Her son is at school, but she is at the school for a meeting.
examples.analysis: The first describes pupil status; the second identifies a location.

examples.sentence: The expedition crossed the Indus before travelling towards Islamabad.
examples.analysis: The river name takes the; the city name normally does not.

examples.sentence: A detailed knowledge of local law would help; knowledge alone is not enough.
examples.analysis: The first has an established qualified count expression; the second is a general noncount use.

contrasts.a: He is in hospital after an operation.
contrasts.b: He is in the hospital after an operation.
contrasts.note: The first is the usual British patient pattern; the second is also the normal American patient pattern, as well as a possible building reference.

exceptions: Institutional zero article is lexical and regional: go to prison does not imply that every prison-related noun phrase must omit the. The prison beside the river needs the when it identifies a building.

mistakes.reason: The ordinary country name Pakistan does not take an article.

mistakes.problem: He gave me a valuable information.
mistakes.reason: Information retains its ordinary noncount pattern despite the adjective valuable.

glossary.definition: Absence of an article in a grammatical noun-phrase construction.
A conventional noun use referring to an institution’s typical activity or participant status.
glossary.example: At school can mean attending as a pupil.

modules.title: Determiners, distribution and quantity
modules.definition: A determiner helps specify reference or quantity within a noun phrase. Articles, demonstratives, possessive determiners, numbers and many quantifiers take part in this system. Their distribution depends on number, countability and the meaning of the construction.
foundation: Demonstratives distinguish near or currently prominent reference from more distant reference: this form, that form, these forms, those forms. Possessive determiners include my, your, her, our and their; they normally replace an article in the central determiner position: my report, not the my report. Whose and which can introduce noun phrases in questions: Which route is open? What kind of evidence is available? In this course, these uses are called determiner uses. Some school descriptions use labels such as demonstrative adjective; identifying the noun-phrase role matters more than confusing terminology with correctness.
intermediate: Cardinal numbers state quantities, such as three rooms; ordinal numbers order members, such as the third room. Quantifiers specify amount or number more loosely: many rooms, much space, several applications and enough evidence. Many combines with plural count nouns; much combines with noncount nouns. Much is especially ordinary in negatives and questions, and also in formal positive phrases such as much research. A lot of can combine with either pattern. Enough precedes a noun but follows an adjective: enough time and clear enough. Its meaning is sufficiency for a stated or understood purpose, not simply a large quantity.
advanced: Each and every distribute attention across individual members: each proposal is different; every proposal needs a signature. Each can stand alone and can occur with of: each of the proposals. Every normally needs a singular count head; use every one of the proposals rather than every of them. Both refers to two together; either selects or permits one of two, and neither excludes the two alternatives. All is not limited to two: all the proposals. These words can interact with negation: not all proposals passed means some did not, whereas no proposals passed excludes every one. Their meanings cannot be reduced to interchangeable substitutes for many.
expert: The of-pattern distinguishes a whole general class from a specified set: many students but many of the students. Compare all students, all the students and all of the students; all allows some patterns that each or several do not. Both my colleagues and both of my colleagues are possible. Distributive quantity and grammatical agreement interact, but agreement receives full treatment on Day 10. Either can also mean both in expressions such as on either side of the road, so interpretation must follow the construction. A determiner is not defined as a word that must always be directly adjacent to its noun; adjectives and other modifiers may intervene.

patterns.meaning: Choose many applicants or much evidence according to the noun’s sense.
Many of the applicants selects from an identified set.

examples.sentence: Each of the three files needs a label.
examples.analysis: Each distributes the requirement to individual files and takes an of-phrase.

examples.sentence: Both our buses have enough space.
examples.analysis: Both identifies the two buses; enough gives a sufficiency judgement about noncount space.

examples.sentence: Not all of the recommendations were adopted.
examples.analysis: Negation excludes complete adoption without saying that none were adopted.

contrasts.note: Both are grammatical; enough says time meets a requirement, while plenty suggests more than sufficient time.

exceptions: Either side of a road can mean each of its two sides. This established construction differs from choosing either of two proposed routes.

mistakes.problem: Every of the forms needs a signature.
mistakes.repair: Every one of the forms needs a signature.
mistakes.reason: Every does not take this of-phrase directly.

mistakes.problem: We have time enough to complete the task. Neutral everyday word order requested.
mistakes.repair: We have enough time to complete the task.
mistakes.reason: Enough normally precedes a noun in neutral prose; time enough is possible in marked or literary contexts and is not universally ungrammatical.

glossary.definition: A meaning that applies separately to members of a set.
An expression indicating number, amount or proportion.
glossary.example: Several, much and all are quantifiers in relevant noun-phrase uses.

modules.title: Some, any, few and little: meaning under quantity and negation
modules.definition: Quantity expressions differ in the expectations they create as well as the nouns they permit. Some and any interact with questions, negation and unrestricted choice; few and little often imply insufficiency, whereas a few and a little present a positive quantity.
foundation: Use a few with plural count nouns and a little with noncount nouns: a few pages, a little time. Removing a changes the usual implication: few pages suggests not many, often fewer than hoped; little time suggests not much. A few and a little assert that some quantity is available, often enough for a modest purpose. The real situation matters: a few mistakes can be reassuring in a long report but serious in a safety procedure. Grammatical form expresses a perspective; it does not calculate whether a quantity is objectively good or bad.
intermediate: Some often introduces an indefinite quantity in an affirmative statement: We bought some paper. Any is common in negatives and open questions: We did not buy any paper; Do you have any paper? These are tendencies, not a rule banning some from questions. Would you like some tea? is an ordinary offer, and Have you got some spare paper? can suggest an expected positive answer. Any also has a free-choice use: Choose any seat means there is no restriction on which seat you select. That use is compatible with a singular count noun.
advanced: In careful edited comparison, fewer commonly accompanies plural count nouns and less accompanies noncount nouns: fewer delays, less disruption. Established exceptions include measurements, sums and time spans regarded as amounts: less than ten minutes and less than twenty pounds. Less is also widespread with plural count nouns, especially in informal usage; a formal editor may prefer fewer ordinary individual items. Do not mark less than five miles wrong by applying a count-noun slogan to a measurement. Meaning and editorial convention are both relevant. More and most do not have separate count and noncount forms.
expert: Scope helps explain quantity expressions that seem similar. I did not read some of the reports can identify a particular subset that went unread, while I did not read any of the reports normally says none were read. Some can be stressed to create a contrast, so intonation and context contribute to interpretation. Few and little are negative in orientation and can license expressions associated with negation: Few applicants have ever complained. A few applicants have complained instead presents an existing positive set. Avoid classifying either sentence by a memorised positive-versus-negative word list without interpreting what is asserted about the set.

patterns.form: few/a few + plural count noun; little/a little + noncount noun
patterns.meaning: The article changes the usual negative or positive orientation.
Ordinarily expresses absence of even one member or amount in that set.

examples.sentence: We have a little fuel, so we can reach the next village.
examples.analysis: A little presents a positive amount, linked here to sufficiency.

examples.sentence: Few applicants had read all the instructions.
examples.analysis: Few presents a small proportion and is negative in orientation.

examples.sentence: The repair took less than thirty minutes but required fewer tools.
examples.analysis: Minutes is a measured span; tools are separate counted objects.

contrasts.note: Both are grammatical. The first emphasises scarcity; the second acknowledges a positive amount.

exceptions: Some is normal in offers and questions with a positive expectation: Would you like some water? Do not replace it automatically with any.

mistakes.problem: There are a little applicants waiting.
mistakes.repair: There are a few applicants waiting.
mistakes.reason: Applicants is a plural count noun, so a few is the compatible expression.
Information is noncount in this ordinary use; little expresses a small amount.

glossary.definition: Any meaning that no particular choice is restricted.
The part of an expression over which a grammatical meaning operates.
glossary.example: Not all does not normally mean none.

questions.prompt: Choose the indefinite article by the following sound: She is ____ honest witness.
questions.why: The indefinite article is an because honest begins with a vowel sound. The is definite, and a singular count use of witness needs an appropriate determiner here.

questions.prompt: Which explanation fits I bought a particular book yesterday?
options: Only the could refer to a specific purchase.
The noun phrase is indefinite but refers to a specific book.
Indefinite always means no particular book exists.
A makes book a noncount noun.
questions.why: The article does not make specificity impossible; particular and the buying context identify the speaker’s intended specific referent.

questions.prompt: Which is the ordinary name of the river in this sentence? We crossed ____.
questions.why: The conventional river name in ordinary reference is the Indus. The alternatives do not give that name in its ordinary use.

questions.prompt: Which is the neutral standard phrase?
questions.why: My occupies the central determiner position; it does not combine with a preceding ordinary article in this noun phrase.

questions.prompt: Complete with an expression meaning a small positive number: We have ____ volunteers, so the event can proceed.
questions.why: A few supplies a positive plural count quantity; a little and much suit noncount nouns, and every requires a singular count phrase.

questions.prompt: Which expression excludes every one of the proposals?
questions.why: No excludes all members. Not all excludes complete acceptance but can allow some; some and a few assert acceptance of members.

questions.prompt: Check the labelled parts in an offer: Would you like [A] / some tea [B] / before we begin [C]? Choose a faulty part or No error.
questions.why: Some is normal in an offer. A rule replacing some with any in every question would reject an established grammatical pattern.

questions.prompt: Which phrase illustrates a conventional comparative for separate counted items, rather than a measured noncount amount?
questions.why: Files are counted individual items, so fewer files gives the relevant count comparison. The other phrases are grammatical comparisons of noncount amounts and do not illustrate this count pattern.

questions.prompt: Which statement about hospital is accurate?
options: In the hospital cannot describe a patient in standard English.
British and American patient expressions must be identical.
In hospital is a usual British patient pattern; in the hospital is a usual American patient pattern.
Every reference to a hospital must have zero article.
questions.why: Institutional article conventions vary by region and construction; neither standard pattern justifies a universal prohibition.

questions.prompt: Which analysis of The violin is difficult to learn is defensible in a general discussion of instruments?
options: The violin can have generic reference to the instrument type.
The always refers to one previously named physical object.
The makes violin a personal pronoun.
Generic statements cannot use the singular.
questions.why: The singular generic construction can present an instrument category; the does not require earlier mention of one physical violin.

questions.prompt: Complete with a/an: ____ useful map; ____ hour; ____ MRI scan.
questions.model: a useful map; an hour; an MRI scan.
rubric: Use the following sound, not the following letter.
Treat MRI as the spoken letters beginning with /em/.
alternatives: Accept another defensible answer that meets each stated requirement and preserves the intended meaning.

questions.prompt: Explain how the kitchen becomes identifiable in We rented a cottage. The kitchen overlooked the garden.
questions.model: The kitchen is inferable as part of the rented cottage, so prior mention of kitchen itself is unnecessary.
rubric: Identify the bridging relationship.
Reject the absolute rule that the requires direct prior mention.
alternatives: Accept another defensible answer that meets each stated requirement and preserves the intended meaning.

questions.prompt: Compare Water is scarce with The water in this tank is contaminated.
questions.model: The first refers to water generally in context; the second identifies a particular quantity using the modifying phrase.
rubric: Connect zero article to general reference.
Explain what identifies the quantity in the second sentence.
alternatives: Accept another defensible answer that meets each stated requirement and preserves the intended meaning.

questions.prompt: Explain at school versus at the school in The child is at school; her parent is at the school for an interview.
questions.model: The first describes participation as a pupil; the second identifies the school location for the parent’s visit.
rubric: Recognise an institutional reading.
Do not claim the parent becomes a pupil merely by being in the building.
alternatives: Accept another defensible answer that meets each stated requirement and preserves the intended meaning.

questions.prompt: Rewrite every of the applicants using a standard distributive of-construction.
rubric: Insert one after every.
Preserve the reference to all individual applicants.
alternatives: each of the applicants is also a suitable alternative if the slight perspective change is acceptable.

questions.prompt: Explain little progress versus a little progress.
questions.model: Little progress emphasises scarcity; a little progress acknowledges some positive progress.
rubric: Preserve progress as noncount.
Explain the contribution of a rather than invent a numerical threshold.
alternatives: Accept another defensible answer that meets each stated requirement and preserves the intended meaning.

questions.prompt: Compare I did not read any of the reports with I did not read some of the reports.
questions.model: The first normally says none were read; the second can identify a subset that was not read.
rubric: Explain the different scope of negation.
Allow context or stress to make the subset reading explicit.
alternatives: Accept another defensible answer that meets each stated requirement and preserves the intended meaning.

questions.prompt: Arrange into a neutral noun phrase: applications / several / the / of.
rubric: Use of before the specified set.
Do not produce several the applications.
alternatives: Accept another defensible answer that meets each stated requirement and preserves the intended meaning.

questions.prompt: Give the normal article pattern for Pakistan, the United Kingdom, the Arabian Sea and Mount Kenya.
questions.model: Pakistan and Mount Kenya normally have zero article; the United Kingdom and the Arabian Sea normally include the.
rubric: Classify the complete conventional names.
Avoid a single rule that all countries or mountains behave identically.
alternatives: Accept another defensible answer that meets each stated requirement and preserves the intended meaning.

questions.prompt: Explain the difference between both proposals and all six proposals.
questions.model: Both refers to two members; all six includes the entire stated set of six.
rubric: Connect both to a two-member set.
Explain all as complete inclusion of the identified set.
alternatives: Accept another defensible answer that meets each stated requirement and preserves the intended meaning.

questions.prompt: Explain any in Choose any seat; there is no assigned seating.
questions.model: Any expresses unrestricted choice from the available seats.
rubric: Identify free choice rather than a negative context.
Connect the interpretation to no assigned seating.
alternatives: Accept another defensible answer that meets each stated requirement and preserves the intended meaning.

questions.prompt: Replace a sufficient amount of time with an enough-phrase, then use enough with clear.
rubric: Place enough before the noun and after the adjective.
Retain sufficiency, not simply abundance.
alternatives: Accept another defensible answer that meets each stated requirement and preserves the intended meaning.

questions.prompt: Introduce a visitor with an indefinite phrase, then refer to the same visitor in a second sentence.
questions.model: A visitor arrived at noon. The visitor asked for the curator.
rubric: Use a/an to introduce one visitor.
Use an identifiable reference to the same visitor afterwards.
alternatives: Accept another defensible answer that meets each stated requirement and preserves the intended meaning.

questions.prompt: Explain why less than five kilometres can be conventional formal English even though kilometres is plural.
questions.model: The expression measures a distance as an amount, an established use of less with numerical measurements.
rubric: Identify the measurement interpretation.
Do not mechanically require fewer for every written plural.
alternatives: Accept another defensible answer that meets each stated requirement and preserves the intended meaning.

questions.prompt: Repair ordinary article/countability errors: She works at an university. She gave us an advice. We visited the Pakistan last year.
questions.model: She works at a university. She gave us advice. We visited Pakistan last year.
rubric: Use the consonant sound at university.
Remove a/an from ordinary noncount advice.
Use the country’s normal article pattern.
alternatives: Accept another defensible answer that meets each stated requirement and preserves the intended meaning.

questions.prompt: Distinguish each proposal is useful from every proposal is useful without inventing a difference in the number included.
questions.model: Both can cover the whole set. Each directs attention to members individually; every generalises across the members.
rubric: Preserve the possible whole-set coverage in both.
Describe emphasis and distribution rather than an absolute logical opposition.
alternatives: Accept another defensible answer that meets each stated requirement and preserves the intended meaning.

questions.prompt: Why is the in the current director compatible with not knowing the director’s personal name?
questions.model: The phrase identifies a unique relevant role; definiteness need not mean familiarity with the person’s name.
rubric: Identify role-based identification.
Keep definiteness distinct from knowing every fact about the referent.
alternatives: Accept another defensible answer that meets each stated requirement and preserves the intended meaning.

questions.prompt: Write an ordinary offer using some and an instruction using free-choice any.
questions.model: Would you like some coffee? Choose any clean cup.
rubric: Use a question whose offer context licenses some.
Use any to remove restrictions on the choice.
alternatives: Accept another defensible answer that meets each stated requirement and preserves the intended meaning.

corrections.prompt: Correct the indefinite article: It is a unusual request.
rubric: Use an before the vowel sound.
Preserve a single request.
alternatives: Accept another defensible answer that meets each stated requirement and preserves the intended meaning.

corrections.prompt: Correct: She submitted the her application yesterday.
rubric: Remove the incompatible ordinary article.
Retain the possessive determiner.
alternatives: Accept another defensible answer that meets each stated requirement and preserves the intended meaning.

corrections.prompt: Correct the quantifier: We need a few equipment.
rubric: Use a noncount-compatible quantity phrase.
Keep equipment in its ordinary sense.
alternatives: We need a few items of equipment.

corrections.prompt: Correct ordinary geographical naming: He lives in United Kingdom.
corrections.model: He lives in the United Kingdom.
rubric: Supply the conventional article.
Keep the full country name.
alternatives: Accept another defensible answer that meets each stated requirement and preserves the intended meaning.

corrections.prompt: Correct: Every of these answers needs checking.
corrections.model: Every one of these answers needs checking.
rubric: Use every one of or a suitable each of construction.
Preserve distributive meaning.
alternatives: Accept another defensible answer that meets each stated requirement and preserves the intended meaning.

corrections.prompt: Correct only if necessary: Would you like some water?
rubric: Recognise an ordinary offer.
Do not replace some solely because this is a question.
alternatives: Accept another defensible answer that meets each stated requirement and preserves the intended meaning.

corrections.prompt: Correct only if necessary: The journey took less than two hours.
rubric: Recognise a measured time span.
Do not impose fewer solely on the written plural hours.
alternatives: Accept another defensible answer that meets each stated requirement and preserves the intended meaning.

corrections.prompt: Use neutral word order: The instructions are enough clear.
rubric: Place enough after the adjective.
Retain sufficiency rather than intensifying to very.
alternatives: Accept another defensible answer that meets each stated requirement and preserves the intended meaning.

transformations.prompt: Rewrite a generic statement about all relevant oak trees using a bare plural: An oak tree needs adequate light.
rubric: Use a bare plural generic subject.
Change agreement to plural without changing the general claim.
alternatives: Accept another defensible answer that meets each stated requirement and preserves the intended meaning.

transformations.prompt: Express that some but not every proposed date is convenient. Start with Not all.
transformations.model: Not all the proposed dates are convenient, but some are.
rubric: Preserve at least one convenient date and at least one inconvenient date.
Begin with Not all and avoid weakening the two-part claim.
alternatives: Accept another defensible answer that meets each stated requirement and preserves the intended meaning.

writing.prompt: Write 80–110 words arranging a small study session. Use first and subsequent mention of a person or object, a zero-article generalisation, a quantity with each or every, some in an offer, and any for free choice. Label the examples.
writing.model:
A tutor has offered to lead a study session on Saturday. The tutor will bring a short passage for discussion and a second copy for anyone who needs larger print. Careful reading matters more than speed in this session. Each participant should bring a notebook and a pen. Would you like some tea before we begin? Choose any seat near the front. We have a little time for questions after the main activity, but some proposed exercises will have to wait until our next meeting.

Analysis: A tutor introduces a referent and the tutor refers back. Careful reading is a zero-article generalisation. Each participant distributes the instruction. Some appears in an offer; any seat permits free choice.
rubric: Use the specified constructions in meaningful contexts.
Keep first/subsequent reference coherent and each/every compatible with its noun.
Explain some as an offer and any as unrestricted choice.
alternatives: Accept another defensible answer that meets each stated requirement and preserves the intended meaning.

recall.prompt: Recall Day 1: distinguish class and function for library in The library closed early.
recall.model: Library is a noun; the whole phrase the library functions as subject.
rubric: Distinguish category from function.
Include the in the full subject phrase.
alternatives: Accept another defensible answer that meets each stated requirement and preserves the intended meaning.

recall.prompt: Recall Day 2: give a count-unit expression for three separate units of furniture.
rubric: Use a countable unit head.
Keep furniture noncount.
alternatives: Accept another defensible answer that meets each stated requirement and preserves the intended meaning.

recall.prompt: Recall Day 2: identify the head in several recent studies of river pollution.
rubric: Distinguish the outer head from pollution.
Keep the postmodifying of-phrase inside the larger noun phrase.
alternatives: Accept another defensible answer that meets each stated requirement and preserves the intended meaning.

checklist: I interpret the intended reference before choosing an article.
I check countability in the particular sense being used.
I can explain both forms when two grammatical constructions differ in meaning.
I recognise some in offers and less with measurements as legitimate.
I preserve negation scope when paraphrasing quantity statements.
